seo.shortDescription: Searchable 2026 U.S. tariff table for all 391 HTS Chapter 64 footwear lines — sneakers, leather shoes, boots, sandals, flip-flops, slippers, shoe parts. Base rates from Free to 48% plus the extra duty by country: Vietnam +12.5%, Indonesia and Cambodia +10%, China up to +20%, Italian leather shoes 10% in total.

overview.intro:
Chapter 64 covers every kind of footwear — rubber and plastic shoes and sandals (6401–6402), leather-upper shoes and boots (6403), textile-upper sneakers and slippers (6404), other footwear (6405) and shoe parts and gaiters (6406). Footwear carries some of the **highest base rates in the tariff schedule**: 369 of the 391 lines are dutiable, and the rate follows the **upper material, the outer sole, the construction and the value per pair**. A men's leather shoe pays 8.5%, a women's 10%; a textile-upper running shoe over $12 a pair 20%; a rubber or plastic shoe under $3 a pair 48%; between $3 and $12 the rate is compound, for example **90¢ a pair + 20%**.

The U.S. imported **$27.19B** of footwear and parts in 2025. **Vietnam** ($9.82B) was the largest supplier, passing China ($7.08B, down 31.1%), ahead of Indonesia, Italy and Cambodia. On top of the base rate comes the **extra duty by country**: since July 24, 2026 a Section 301 tariff on 60 economies — **+12.5% for Vietnam and Thailand, +10% for Indonesia, Cambodia and India**, and **10% in total for Italian, Spanish and other EU shoes** (nothing added where the base rate is already 10% or more). **China** pays +12.5% plus **+7.5% (List 4A)** on 242 of the 391 lines. **Japanese leather shoes** still pay a **40% duty imposed in 1986**, and Brazil +37.5%. USMCA-qualifying footwear from Mexico and Canada pays nothing, except women's leather ankle boots from Canada (6403.91.90), which owe a **50% Section 338 duty even under USMCA**.

productGroups.label: Waterproof rubber & plastic footwear (rain boots, galoshes, molded boots)
productGroups.blurb: Boots and overshoes whose rubber or plastic upper is molded or cemented to the sole, not stitched — rain boots, rubber "duck" boots, galoshes. Most pay 37.5%; galoshes without closures 25%; boots almost all of PVC (over 90% of the surface) 4.6%; ski and snowboard boots Free.

productGroups.label: Other rubber & plastic footwear (sneakers, sandals, flip-flops, clogs, slides)
productGroups.blurb: The widest range in the chapter. Zoris and flip-flops with plugged straps (6402.20) are Free, one-piece molded plastic sandals 3%, and shoes whose upper is over 90% rubber or plastic without a foxing band 6%. Other rubber and plastic shoes pay by value: 48% under $3 a pair, 90¢/pr. + 37.5% for $3–$6.50, 90¢/pr. + 20% for $6.50–$12, and 20% over $12; protective active footwear (hiking and trail shoes over $24 with a coated or laminated waterproof textile) 20%.

productGroups.label: Leather-upper footwear (dress shoes, boots, leather sneakers, sandals)
productGroups.blurb: Shoes and boots with leather uppers. Men's leather shoes pay 8.5%, women's and children's 10%, welt-constructed shoes 5%, turn footwear 2.5%; leather sandals with straps (6403.20) and women's leather sports shoes (6403.19.70) are Free. Japanese leather shoes also pay a 40% duty dating from 1986.

productGroups.label: Textile-upper footwear (athletic and canvas sneakers, slippers, espadrilles)
productGroups.blurb: Shoes with textile uppers. Rubber- or plastic-soled athletic and canvas sneakers pay 20% over $12 a pair and compound or 37.5%–48% rates below $12; other textile shoes over $12 pay 9%. Slippers and espadrilles whose outer sole touches the ground mostly with textile pay 7.5%–12.5%. Textile shoes with leather soles 10%–37.5%.

productGroups.label: Other footwear (wood, felt, cork, disposable, other uppers)
productGroups.blurb: Footwear not covered above — wooden clogs and shoes with uppers of leather on other soles 10%, textile uppers 7.5%–12.5%, wool felt 2.5%, disposable footwear 3.8%.

productGroups.label: Footwear parts (uppers, outer soles, insoles) and gaiters, leg-warmers
productGroups.blurb: Uppers, soles and other parts. Formed textile uppers pay like finished shoes — 33.6% under $3 a pair, 63¢/pr. + 26.2% for $3–$6.50 — leather formed uppers 8.5%–10%; non-formed leather, rubber and plastic uppers are Free; rubber or plastic outer soles and heels 2.7%; removable insoles and other parts of rubber or plastics 5.3%; textile gaiters and leg-warmers 14.9%.

workedExamples.title: Textile running shoes from Vietnam, over $12 a pair
workedExamples.body: Athletic shoes with rubber or plastic soles and textile uppers valued over $12 a pair pay 20%. Vietnam adds +12.5% (9903.05.84): **32.5%**, $3,250 on a $10,000 shipment. The same shoes pay 30% from Indonesia, Cambodia or India, 20% from the EU (the base rate is already over 10%), and 40% from China, because 6404.11.90 is on List 4A (+12.5% + 7.5%). In late 2025 they paid 40% from Vietnam (20% IEEPA).

workedExamples.title: Same sneaker, $10 a pair — the compound rate
workedExamples.body: Below $12 a pair the rate is per pair plus a percentage: 90¢/pr. + 20%. For 1,000 pairs at $10 ($10,000) that is $900 + $2,000 = $2,900, 29% of value. From Vietnam add +12.5% of value: **$4,150 (41.5%)**. Under $3 a pair the same kind of shoe pays 48% (6404.11.59), so cheap sneakers pay a higher share of their price than expensive ones.

workedExamples.title: Women's leather shoes from Italy
workedExamples.body: Women's leather-upper shoes with rubber or plastic soles valued over $2.50 a pair pay 10%. For EU goods the 2026 Section 301 action charges 10% in total (9903.05.39), and the base rate is already 10%, so nothing is added: **$1,000 on $10,000**. A men's pair (6403.99.60, 8.5%) also pays 10% in total from Italy. From Brazil the women's pair pays 47.5%; from Japan 52.5% — 12.5% in total plus the 40% 1986 duty.

workedExamples.title: Women's leather ankle boots from Canada
workedExamples.body: The base rate is 10%, and USMCA-qualifying goods pay neither the base rate nor the 10% Section 301 duty (9903.05.93). But 6403.91.90 is on the Section 338 list in U.S. note 51(b)(3) (9903.03.14), which applies even when USMCA is claimed: **$5,000** on a $10,000 shipment. A non-qualifying shipment pays 10% + 10% + 50% = 70%. Men's boots (6403.91.60) are not on the list.

workedExamples.title: Flip-flops from China
workedExamples.body: Zoris — flip-flops whose straps are plugged through the sole — are Free. 6402.20 was on China's List 4B, which was suspended before it took effect, so Chinese flip-flops pay only the 2026 Section 301 duty: **12.5%**. One-piece molded plastic sandals (6402.99.27) pay 3%, plus 12.5% from China, and are on List 4A, so 23%.

notes.chapterNotes:
**Note 1.** This chapter does not cover: (a) disposable foot or shoe coverings of flimsy material (for example, paper, sheeting of plastics) without applied soles — these are classified according to their constituent material; (b) footwear of textile material, without an outer sole glued, sewn or otherwise affixed or applied to the upper (section XI); (c) worn footwear of heading 6309; (d) articles of asbestos (heading 6812); (e) orthopedic footwear or other orthopedic appliances, or parts thereof (heading 9021; see heading 9817.64.01); or (f) toy footwear or skating boots with ice or roller skates attached; shin-guards or similar protective sportswear (chapter 95).

**Note 2.** For heading 6406, "parts" does not include pegs, protectors, eyelets, hooks, buckles, ornaments, braid, laces, pompons or other trimmings (classified in their own headings) or buttons or other goods of heading 9606.

**Note 3.** In this chapter (a) "rubber" and "plastics" include woven fabrics or other textile products with an external layer of rubber or plastics visible to the naked eye (any resulting change of color is ignored); and (b) "leather" means the goods of headings 4107 and 4112 to 4114.

**Note 4.** Subject to note 3: (a) the material of the upper is the constituent material with the greatest external surface area, ignoring accessories or reinforcements such as ankle patches, edging, ornamentation, buckles, tabs, eyelet stays or similar attachments; (b) the material of the outer sole is the material with the greatest surface area in contact with the ground, ignoring accessories or reinforcements such as spikes, bars, nails, protectors or similar attachments.

**Subheading note 1.** For subheadings 6402.12, 6402.19, 6403.12, 6403.19 and 6404.11, "sports footwear" applies only to (a) footwear designed for a sporting activity that has, or has provision for the attachment of, spikes, sprigs, cleats, stops, clips, bars or the like; and (b) skating boots, ski-boots and cross-country ski footwear, snowboard boots, wrestling boots, boxing boots and cycling shoes.
notes.additionalUsNotes:
**1.** (a) "Welt footwear" means footwear constructed with a welt that extends around the edge of the tread portion of the sole, in which the welt and shoe upper are sewed to a lip on the surface of the insole, and the outsole is sewed or cemented to the welt; (b) "footwear for men, youths and boys" covers footwear of American youths' size 11-1/2 and larger for males, and does not include footwear commonly worn by both sexes.

**2.** "Tennis shoes, basketball shoes, gym shoes, training shoes and the like" covers athletic footwear other than sports footwear (as defined in subheading note 1), whether or not principally used for such athletic games or purposes.

**3.** For heading 6401, "waterproof footwear" means footwear specified in the heading, designed to protect against penetration by water or other liquids, whether or not primarily designed for such purposes.

**4.** "Formed uppers" (subheading 6406.10) are uppers with closed bottoms that have been shaped by lasting, molding or otherwise, but not by simply closing at the bottom.

**5.** In finding the material of the outer sole under note 4(b), textile materials that lack the characteristics usually required for normal use of an outer sole, including durability and strength, are not taken into account.

**6.** For subheadings 6402.91.42 and 6402.99.32, "protective active footwear" means footwear (other than sports footwear) designed for outdoor activities, such as hiking shoes, trekking shoes, running shoes and trail running shoes, valued over $24 a pair, that provides protection against water imparted by a coated or laminated textile fabric.

**Statistical notes.** "Work footwear" (statistical note 1(a)) covers footwear with a metal toe-cap and specialized footwear with rubber or plastic outer soles designed for occupations such as agriculture, construction, industry, public safety and transportation, with features that protect against workplace hazards; "house slippers" (note 1(d)) are footwear with very thin outer soles (cellular rubber, non-grain leather or textile up to 3.5 mm; PVC up to 2 mm) or sole components not over 8 mm thick at the ball with no higher heel.

tariffUpdates.h1: HTS Chapter 64: Footwear, Shoes & Boots — Tariff Updates

seo.title: Shoe Tariffs 2026: HTS Chapter 64 Footwear Tariff Updates Since January 2025 — China, Vietnam, Indonesia, Italy | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: What changed for U.S. footwear tariffs since January 2025: the end of the IEEPA and Section 122 duties, the 2026 Section 301 tariffs (Vietnam +12.5%, Indonesia and Cambodia +10%, EU 10% in total), China List 4A, Japan's 1986 leather-footwear duty, Canada Section 338 and the end of de minimis, with Federal Register citations.

tariffUpdates.intro:
This page compares two editions of the tariff schedule: the **2025 Basic Edition**, in force at the start of 2025, and the current **2026 Revision 21** (in force October 9, 2026). **No Chapter 64 base rate changed**: all 391 lines carry the same General, Special and Column 2 rates, from Free to 48% and compound rates such as 90¢/pr. + 37.5%.

Everything that changed sits on top of the base rate. In 2025 the IEEPA duties reached footwear from every country — 20% for Vietnam, 19% for Indonesia, Cambodia and Thailand, 15% in total for the EU from August 7, 2025, 50% for India and Brazil from August 2025, and up to 145% for China in April–May 2025, on top of the 7.5% List 4A duty. The IEEPA duties **ended on February 24, 2026** (importers can now claim refunds through CBP's CAPE process), and the 10% Section 122 surcharge that replaced them expired on July 23, 2026. Since **July 24, 2026** goods from 60 economies pay a **Section 301 tariff**: +12.5% for Vietnam and Thailand, +10% for Indonesia, Cambodia and India, 10% in total for the EU and 12.5% in total for Japan. China still pays **+7.5% (List 4A)** on 242 of the 391 lines, Japan the **40% duty of 1986** on leather footwear, and since **August 22, 2026** Canadian women's leather ankle boots (6403.91.90) a **50% Section 338 duty**, even under USMCA. The $800 de minimis exemption stays suspended, so shoes shipped direct to consumers pay full duty.
tariffUpdates.scope: Measures that reach Chapter 64 from any country: the 2026 Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies, the Brazil Section 301 tariff, the China Section 301 List 4A duty (and the suspended List 4B), the 1986 Section 301 duty on leather footwear from Japan (9903.41.10), the Canada Section 338 duty, Russia's rates in lieu of column 2, the Nicaragua Section 301 duty scheduled for 2027, the 2025–2026 IEEPA and Section 122 duties that have ended, and the suspension of de minimis. Preference-program changes (AGOA, GSP) are listed for reference. No antidumping or countervailing duty order covers a Chapter 64 product. For the rate each supplier pays, see Rates by country.

changes.detail: USTR announced that the China Section 301 actions did not terminate on their anniversaries because domestic industries asked for them to continue. For Chapter 64 this keeps +7.5% (List 4A, 9903.88.15) on 242 lines; List 4B stays suspended.

changes.title: Canada Section 338 lists revised; Chapter 64 entry unchanged
changes.detail: Proclamations 11064 and 11065 added and removed provisions on the Section 338 lists. None of the added or removed provisions is in Chapter 64, so 6403.91.90 stays on the 9903.03.14 list. From this date the duty also applies on top of any Section 232 duty.

changes.title: Canada Section 338 duty takes effect on women's leather ankle boots (6403.91.90)
changes.detail: 50% on listed products of Canada after a 3-day suspension lapsed. The only Chapter 64 provision on the motor-vehicle list (9903.03.14, U.S. note 51(b)(3)) is 6403.91.90 — leather-upper footwear covering the ankle, for women and other persons, with outer soles of rubber, plastics or composition leather (4 statistical lines). Unlike the Section 301 duty, it applies to USMCA-qualifying goods too (U.S. note 51(a)).

changes.title: Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies cover all of Chapter 64
changes.detail: 10% or 12.5% on all products of 60 economies (9903.05.20–9903.05.84). No Chapter 64 line is on the general exemption list (note 52(b)) or on any country exception list (note 52(j)). Vietnam, Thailand, China and the Philippines +12.5%; Indonesia, Cambodia, India, Bangladesh and Pakistan +10%. EU goods pay 10% in total and Japanese 12.5% in total — nothing extra on lines already at or above that rate. CAFTA-DR footwear pays it too. USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico are exempt (9903.05.93, 9903.05.94).

changes.title: Section 122 import surcharge expired
changes.detail: The 150-day surcharge (9903.03.01) expired at the close of July 23, 2026.

changes.title: Section 301 tariff on products of Brazil
changes.detail: 25% on all goods of Brazil (9903.05.01). No Chapter 64 line is on the Brazil exemption list (U.S. note 50(a)(ii)). From July 24 the 12.5% forced-labor tariff (9903.05.27) is added on top.

changes.title: USMCA joint review: not renewed, still in force
changes.detail: The United States did not agree to renew the USMCA in its current form. USTR said the Agreement remains in force pending resolution of the issues or until termination, so USMCA claims (SPI S) still remove the base rate and the Section 301 duty on Mexican and Canadian footwear.

changes.title: CBP suspends de minimis indefinitely
changes.detail: Two interim final rules suspend the $800 de minimis exemption in CBP's regulations: 19 CFR 10.151(b) for every mode except mail, and 19 CFR 145.31(b) for mail, until CBP announces otherwise. A pair of shoes shipped direct to a U.S. consumer needs an entry and pays the full duty — base rate plus the extra duty for its origin. The new postal informal entry process took effect July 24, 2026.

changes.title: CBP opens CAPE for IEEPA duty refunds
changes.detail: CBP deployed the Consolidated Administration and Processing of Entries (CAPE) function in ACE: importers of record and their brokers file a CAPE Declaration listing entries, and ACE removes the IEEPA Chapter 99 lines and refunds the IEEPA duties with interest, generally within 60–90 days. Phase 1 covers unliquidated entries and entries still within the voluntary reliquidation period. The Section 301, List 4A, 1986 Japan and Section 338 duties are not refunded.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge replaces the IEEPA tariffs
changes.detail: 10% on products of all countries (9903.03.01) until July 23, 2026. No Chapter 64 subheading was on the product exemption lists (9903.03.03–9903.03.06). USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico were exempt (9903.03.07, 9903.03.08).

changes.title: All IEEPA tariffs end
changes.detail: After the Supreme Court held on February 20, 2026 (Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump) that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, Executive Order 14389 ended the Canada, Mexico, China, Brazil, India and reciprocal duties, and CBP stopped collecting them for goods entered from 12:00 a.m. ET on February 24. The 9903.01.xx and 9903.02.xx headings are still printed in Revision 21 but are no longer in effect.

changes.title: De minimis suspension continued after the IEEPA ruling
changes.detail: Executive Order 14388 kept duty-free de minimis treatment suspended for all countries.

changes.title: India's extra 25% IEEPA duty removed
changes.detail: Executive Order 14384 ended the additional 25% duty on products of India (9903.01.84) from February 7, 2026. The 25% reciprocal rate on India ended with the other IEEPA duties on February 24.

changes.title: AGOA reauthorized through December 31, 2026
changes.detail: The Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (P.L. 119-75) renewed AGOA retroactively from September 30, 2025. AGOA (SPI D) makes most dutiable Chapter 64 lines Free for eligible sub-Saharan countries — footwear is one of the import-sensitive goods AGOA may cover although GSP may not. GSP (SPI A) remains expired since December 31, 2020 and never covered most footwear.

changes.title: Scheduled: Section 301 tariff on products of Nicaragua
changes.detail: USTR's implementation notice: products of Nicaragua that pay the column 1-general rate (that is, not entered under CAFTA-DR) will pay +10% (9903.89.01) from January 1, 2027 and +15% from January 1, 2028, on every Chapter 64 line. Today Nicaragua pays the 12.5% 2026 Section 301 duty (9903.05.58).

changes.title: China fentanyl duty cut to 10%
changes.detail: The IEEPA duty on products of China and Hong Kong (9903.01.24) fell from +20% to +10%. It ended with the other IEEPA duties on February 24, 2026.

changes.title: De minimis exemption suspended for all countries
changes.detail: Executive Order 14324 ended duty-free entry for shipments valued at $800 or less from every country, effective for goods entered from August 29, 2025. Direct-to-consumer shoe parcels have paid duty since then.

changes.title: Extra 25% on products of India
changes.detail: Executive Order 14329 added 25% on Indian goods (9903.01.84), on top of the 25% reciprocal rate in force since August 7, 2025 (EO 14326): 50% in all on Indian footwear, on top of the base rate. Ended February 7, 2026.

changes.title: Country reciprocal rates replace the 10% baseline
changes.detail: Executive Order 14326 set country rates for goods entered from August 7, 2025: Indonesia, Cambodia, Thailand, Pakistan and the Philippines +19%, Vietnam, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka +20%, India +25%, Myanmar +40%, the UK +10%. EU goods with a column 1 rate under 15% paid 15% in total (9903.02.20) — so Italian leather shoes paid 15%, while EU textile and plastic shoes already at 20% or more paid nothing extra. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Extra 40% on products of Brazil
changes.detail: Executive Order 14323 added 40% on Brazilian goods, on top of the 10% reciprocal duty: 50% in all on Brazilian footwear, on top of the base rate. Footwear was not on its exemption list. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Canada additional duty raised to 35%
changes.detail: Raised the IEEPA duty on non-USMCA Canadian goods to +35% (9903.01.10). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Law ends the de minimis exemption from July 1, 2027
changes.detail: Section 70531 of P.L. 119-21 terminates the de minimis exemption of 19 U.S.C. 1321(a)(2)(C) effective July 1, 2027, as CBP's 2026 rules note.

changes.title: China reciprocal duty cut from 125% to 10%
changes.detail: Executive Order 14298 cut the reciprocal duty on Chinese goods to 10% for goods entered from May 14, 2025. A Chinese textile running shoe over $12 a pair then paid 20% + 7.5% (List 4A) + 20% + 10% = 57.5% until November 9, 2025. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: China reciprocal duty raised to 125%
changes.detail: Executive Order 14266 raised the reciprocal duty on Chinese goods to 125% from April 10, 2025, and paused the higher country rates announced on April 2 for other countries (Vietnam 46%, Cambodia 49%, Indonesia 32%), which never took effect. With the 20% fentanyl duty and the 7.5% List 4A duty, a Chinese textile running shoe over $12 (20% base) paid 172.5% until May 13, 2025.

changes.title: Reciprocal tariff on products of all countries
changes.detail: 10% baseline (9903.01.25) from April 5, 2025, and country rates (9903.02.xx); Canada and Mexico excluded. No Chapter 64 product was exempt. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: China fentanyl duty raised to 20%
changes.detail: The IEEPA duty on products of China and Hong Kong (9903.01.20, then 9903.01.24) went from +10% (from February 4, 2025) to +20%, on top of the List 4A duty. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Additional duty on products of Mexico
changes.detail: +25% on non-USMCA goods (9903.01.01); USMCA-qualifying goods exempt (9903.01.04). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Additional duty on products of Canada
changes.detail: +25% on non-USMCA goods (9903.01.10), later raised to +35%; USMCA-qualifying goods exempt (9903.01.14). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: China List 4A duty cut to 7.5%
changes.detail: Under the Phase One agreement USTR cut the List 4A duty (9903.88.15) from 15% to 7.5%. The rate on the 242 Chapter 64 lines has been 7.5% ever since.

changes.title: China List 4B suspended before it took effect
changes.detail: USTR suspended indefinitely the 15% List 4B duty (9903.88.16) that was to start December 15, 2019. List 4B held 56 Chapter 64 subheadings — among them flip-flops, plastic-upper shoes without foxing, protective active footwear, adhesive-soled textile sneakers and many textile slippers — so those Chinese shoes never paid a China Section 301 list duty.

changes.title: China Section 301 List 4A reaches footwear
changes.detail: The fourth China Section 301 list put +15% on 91 Chapter 64 subheadings: most leather-upper footwear, rain boots, many rubber, plastic and textile shoes and most shoe parts. No Chapter 64 line was on Lists 1–3.

changes.title: Japan footwear duty carried into the HTS as 9903.41.10
changes.detail: Proclamation 5911 moved the 1986 duty into the new Harmonized Tariff Schedule as heading 9903.41.10, with U.S. note 3 to Chapter 99 subchapter III making it cumulative with all other duties. Revision 21 still prints it, and U.S. note 5 does not list it among the suspended headings.

changes.title: USTR rewrites the footwear item of the Japan duty
changes.detail: A USTR notice replaced the footwear description, back to March 31, 1986, with the text that 9903.41.10 still carries: leather footwear and footwear with uppers predominantly of leather, except indoor slip-ons with thin flat soles and sports footwear such as cleated, ski, skating, wrestling, boxing and cycling footwear. It did not end the duty.

changes.title: 40% Section 301 duty on leather footwear from Japan
changes.detail: Proclamation 5448 (signed March 16, 1986) added 40% ad valorem to leather footwear and leather from Japan, in response to Japan's quotas on imports of U.S. leather and footwear. It lets USTR suspend or end the duty only by a notice in the Federal Register, and none has done so.

understandIndustry.why:
U.S. imports of footwear and parts were **$27.19B in 2025**, 4.2% less than the $28.39B of 2024 and well below the $37.97B peak of 2022. Leather-upper footwear (heading 6403) was the largest group at $11.44B (42%), followed by textile-upper footwear (6404, $7.95B) and rubber and plastic footwear (6402, $6.39B). The largest single product was **leather-upper shoes with rubber or plastic soles not covering the ankle (6403.99)**, $6.22B, then **rubber and plastic shoes (6402.99)**, $4.91B, and **textile athletic shoes (6404.11)**, $4.28B.

The supplier map moved away from China. **Vietnam** supplied $9.82B (36.1%, +7.5%), up from $6.73B in 2020, and passed China as the largest supplier for the first time in 2020–2025. **China** fell 31.1% to $7.08B, from $10.28B in 2024. **Indonesia** ($3.06B, +16.0%) and **Cambodia** ($1.40B, +49.9%) more than doubled their 2020 levels, and Bangladesh ($394M, +56.6%) and India ($526M) grew too. **Italy** ($2.02B), Germany, Portugal and Spain — $2.97B together — ship mostly leather-upper shoes (6403), as do Mexico, India and Bangladesh; most of Vietnam's shipments are textile and leather shoes, China's rubber, plastic and textile shoes. Mexico ($748M) and Canada ($44.1M) supplied 2.9% of 2025 imports, and Brazil $231M.

The figures are annual and stop at 2025, before the 2026 tariff changes (the end of the IEEPA duties in February, the Section 301 tariffs from July 24, 2026 and the Canada Section 338 duty from August 22); they do not show what those changes did. Duty-collected figures are not available from an official source yet.

industryAreas.intro:
Footwear base rates are among the highest in the tariff schedule, and the extra duty **depends on where the shoes come from**. Each cell below is the base rate for that product group plus the extra duty for that country, minus any preference — taken from the current tariff schedule.

Since the IEEPA duties ended on February 24, 2026, the extra duty is mainly the **Section 301 tariff on 60 economies** that started July 24, 2026: **+12.5% for Vietnam and Thailand**, **+10% for Indonesia, Cambodia and India**, and **10% in total for Italy, Spain, Portugal and the rest of the EU** — which adds nothing to EU rubber, plastic or textile shoes already at 10% or more. **China adds 12.5%, or 20% on the 242 List 4A lines.** **Japan** has a 12.5% floor plus the **40% duty of 1986 on leather footwear**, and **Brazil** pays +37.5%. USMCA-qualifying shoes from Mexico and Canada pay nothing, except Canadian women's leather ankle boots (6403.91.90), which owe the **50% Section 338 duty** whatever is claimed.

tariffEngineering.h1: HTS Chapter 64: Footwear, Shoes & Boots — Import Documents & Ways to Lower Duty

seo.title: Importing Shoes into the U.S.: Footwear Invoice Rules, Marking, Exotic Leather & Legal Ways to Lower Duty (HTS Ch. 64) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: What each HTS Chapter 64 footwear line needs at U.S. entry — the 19 CFR 141.89 footwear invoice details, country-of-origin marking, FWS and CITES rules for python, ostrich or alligator boots, CPSC rules for children's shoes — and the legal ways to pay less: upper and sole material, foxing, origin, USMCA, AGOA, CAFTA-DR, first sale, drawback, FTZ and rulings.
keywords: external surface area of the upper

tariffEngineering.intro:
Footwear needs no import license, but it does need **more paperwork than most goods**: CBP requires every footwear invoice (headings 6401–6405) to state the style number, the share of the **upper's external surface** that is leather, rubber or plastics, or textile, the outer sole's material, and answers on construction — waterproofing, foxing, metal toe-caps, value per pair — because those facts decide the line. Every shoe must be **marked with its country of origin**. Boots and shoes of **exotic leather** (python, alligator, ostrich, stingray) are wildlife products that need Fish and Wildlife Service clearance, and **children's shoes** must meet CPSC lead and certification rules.

On cost, the schedule leaves real room: the **upper and sole materials, the foxing and the value per pair** decide a base rate between Free and 48%, the **country of origin** decides the extra duty (+10% Indonesia, +12.5% Vietnam, up to +20% China, +40% more for Japanese leather shoes), and USMCA, AGOA, CAFTA-DR, first-sale valuation, drawback and foreign-trade zones lower the bill further. Each lever depends on a document, listed below with its regulation.

levers.title: Know what decides the line: the upper and the outer sole
levers.saves: The gap between material rates: a women's leather shoe pays 10% (6403.99.90), the same design with a textile upper 20% over $12 a pair (6404.11.90) or 90¢/pr. + 20% for $6.50–$12, and with a rubber or plastic upper 20% (6402.99.90); a textile-upper sneaker whose leather overlays and reinforcements cover over 50% of the upper 10.5% (6404.11.20)
levers.appliesTo: Headings 6402, 6403 and 6404 — sneakers, casual and dress shoes, boots
levers.document: A specification sheet with the percentage of the upper's external surface area by material and the outer sole's material in contact with the ground — the same figures 19 CFR 141.89 requires on the invoice.
levers.caveat: Accessories and reinforcements (ankle patches, eyelet stays, edging, ornaments) are not counted (note 4(a)), and a textile with a visible rubber or plastic layer counts as rubber or plastics (note 3(a)). CBP measures the external surface itself; the shoe must really be built the way it is declared.

levers.title: Foxing, textile outer soles and the "over 90% rubber" lines
levers.saves: Shoes whose upper is over 90% rubber or plastic and that have no foxing or foxing-like band pay 6% (6402.91.40, 6402.99.31) instead of 20%–48% or 90¢/pr. + 20%–37.5%. Textile shoes valued up to $12 a pair whose outer sole touches the ground mostly with a durable textile pay 7.5%–12.5% (for example 6404.19.37, .47, .57, .77, .87) instead of 37.5%–48% or compound rates.
levers.appliesTo: Rubber and plastic footwear (6402) and textile-upper footwear with rubber or plastic soles (6404.11, 6404.19)
levers.document: Drawings and samples showing how far any band at the sole overlaps the upper and how much of the perimeter it encircles, and the ground-contact area of the outer sole by material.
levers.caveat: CBP treats a band molded or applied at the sole that overlaps the upper by about 1/4 inch (adult sizes) and encircles 60% or more of the perimeter as foxing-like; 41%–59% depends on the shoe, and 40% or less is not. Textile on the sole that lacks the durability and strength of a real outer sole is ignored (additional U.S. note 5). Over $12 a pair, most textile shoes pay 9% or 20% whatever the sole.

citations.label: CBP Informed Compliance Publication: Footwear (foxing-like bands)

levers.title: Know the country of origin — and where a shoe gets it
levers.saves: The difference between country rates: +10% for Indonesia, Cambodia or India, +12.5% for Vietnam or Thailand, 10% in total for the EU, +20% for China on List 4A lines, +37.5% for Brazil, +40% more for Japanese leather shoes
levers.appliesTo: All lines; the gap is widest on leather shoes from Japan or Brazil and sneakers from China
levers.document: Production records showing where the shoe was last substantially transformed — typically where the upper is lasted and attached to the outer sole; for goods of Canada or Mexico, the part 102 tariff-shift rules.
levers.caveat: Only cutting, packing, labeling or adding trim in a third country does not move the origin. The Section 301, 1986 Japan and Section 338 duties follow the country of origin, and CBP can ask for proof.

citations.label: 19 CFR 102.11 (origin of goods of Canada and Mexico)
HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. notes 3, 20, 51, 52

levers.title: Claim USMCA on footwear from Mexico or Canada
levers.saves: The base rate (up to 48%) plus the 10% Section 301 duty
levers.appliesTo: All lines from Mexico; from Canada, every line except 6403.91.90 (women's leather ankle boots), which keeps the 50% Section 338 duty
levers.document: A certification of origin from the importer, exporter or producer, kept ready for CBP.
levers.caveat: USMCA does not remove the 50% Section 338 duty on 6403.91.90 (U.S. note 51(a)). The shoe must meet the Chapter 64 rule of origin in General Note 11: a change from any heading outside 6401–6405 except formed uppers of 6406.10, plus at least 55% regional value content (net cost method). The USMCA was not renewed at the July 1, 2026 joint review but remains in force.

citations.label: HTSUS General Note 11 (USMCA rules of origin)

levers.title: Claim AGOA, CAFTA-DR, CBTPA or another FTA
levers.saves: The base rate — up to 48% or 90¢/pr. + 37.5%
levers.appliesTo: Dutiable lines whose Special column lists the program: AGOA (D, sub-Saharan Africa, to December 31, 2026), CAFTA-DR (P), CBTPA (R, Haiti and other Caribbean beneficiaries, through September 30, 2030), Jordan (JO), Korea (KR) and the other FTA partners
levers.document: The origin proof each program requires (a certification or declaration of origin, or the AGOA/CBTPA documentation) and records to back it up.
levers.caveat: An FTA removes the base rate but not the 2026 Section 301 duty of a listed country (U.S. note 52(a)) — CAFTA-DR shoes from the Dominican Republic still pay 12.5%, from Guatemala, El Salvador or Honduras 10%. AGOA footwear from a beneficiary outside the 60 (for example Kenya) is duty-free; from South Africa, Nigeria or Angola it still pays 12.5%. GSP (A) never covered most footwear and has been expired since December 31, 2020.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 52(a), (i)

levers.title: Value at the first sale for export when you buy through a middleman
levers.saves: Every ad valorem duty is charged on a lower value — the base rate and the 10%–52.5% extra duties included — when the factory price to a trading company or brand owner is lower than the price you pay. The value per pair can also decide the line, so the first-sale price may move a shoe into a different value bracket.
levers.appliesTo: All lines bought through a trading company, agent-buyer or brand owner rather than straight from the factory
levers.document: Proof that the first sale was a bona fide sale for export to the United States at arm's length: the factory invoice, contracts and payment records.
levers.caveat: Only a sale clearly destined for the U.S. qualifies, and the importer must be able to show the earlier price at entry. The per-pair part of a compound rate does not change with value.

levers.title: Use a Chapter 98 provision: post-surgery footwear, U.S. parts, returned goods
levers.saves: Made-to-measure single shoes for supporting the foot after an illness, operation or injury are Free (9817.64.01) and, as a Chapter 98 entry, skip the 2026 Section 301 duty. Shoes assembled abroad from U.S.-made components (for example uppers cut in the U.S.) pay duty only on the value added abroad (9802.00.80). U.S.-made shoes returned unchanged pay nothing (9801.00.10).
levers.appliesTo: Medical footwear presented singly; footwear assembled from U.S. components; American footwear coming back
levers.document: For 9817.64.01, evidence the shoe is made to measure and presented singly; for 9802.00.80, the assembler's declaration and the cost of the U.S. components (19 CFR 10.24); for 9801.00.10, proof of U.S. origin and export.
levers.caveat: Under 9802.00.80 the Section 301 duty still applies to the value of the assembly abroad (U.S. note 52(a)). Orthopedic appliances of heading 9021 are not Chapter 64 goods.

provisions.text: Footwear, other than goods of heading 9021, for supporting or holding the foot after an illness, operation or injury, made to measure and presented singly, designed to fit either foot

provisions.rate: Duty on full value less U.S. components
provisions.text: Articles assembled abroad from fabricated U.S. components
Products of the United States returned without having been advanced in value or improved

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 52(a)

levers.title: Recover duty on shoes you export or destroy
levers.saves: Up to 99% of the duties paid, when the imported footwear is exported (for example to Canadian or Latin American stores) or destroyed under CBP supervision
levers.appliesTo: Any line that paid a duty
levers.document: A drawback claim to CBP with import and export (or destruction) records that tie the goods together.
levers.caveat: Claims have filing deadlines and record-keeping rules; check whether a given Chapter 99 duty is eligible before relying on it.

levers.title: Hold, sort or relabel shoes in a foreign-trade zone
levers.saves: No duty on footwear re-exported from the zone, and duty deferred until shoes leave it for the U.S. market
levers.appliesTo: Any line — useful for distribution centers that also ship to Canada and Mexico
levers.document: Zone admission (CBP Form 214) and the zone operator's inventory records.
levers.caveat: Shoes entered for U.S. consumption from a zone pay the duties in force on the entry date.

levers.title: Claim back IEEPA duties paid in 2025–2026
levers.saves: The IEEPA duties paid on footwear entered between February 2025 and February 23, 2026 — for example 20% on Vietnamese or 19% on Indonesian shoes — with interest
levers.appliesTo: Past entries of any line that paid an IEEPA duty (9903.01.xx, 9903.02.xx)
levers.document: A CAPE Declaration filed in the ACE Portal by the importer of record or its customs broker, listing the entries, plus ACH refund details on file.
levers.caveat: Phase 1 covers unliquidated entries and entries within the voluntary reliquidation period; other entries may need a protest or court action. It does not refund Section 301, List 4A, the 1986 Japan duty or Section 338.

levers.title: Get a binding classification ruling
levers.saves: Certainty where the line decides the rate and the extra duty: leather versus textile upper, foxing or not, athletic or not, house slipper or not, work footwear, protective active footwear; and whether a Japanese shoe falls in the 1986 exceptions
levers.appliesTo: Any line where the material, construction or use decides the line
levers.document: A ruling request to CBP describing the shoe, with a sample and the external surface and sole percentages.
levers.caveat: Rulings apply to the shoe described; a changed design or material may need a new one.

rules.title: Footwear invoices (headings 6401–6405) must give the manufacturer's and importer's style numbers, the percentage of the upper's external surface that is leather, composition leather, rubber or plastics, textile or other material, the same for the outer sole, and the answers to CBP's construction questions (waterproof, protective metal toe-cap, foxing, value per pair and others)

Country-of-origin marking in English, legible, indelible and permanent enough to reach the ultimate purchaser — on each shoe (usually a label or stamp inside), or on the container where an exception applies; a U.S. place name or brand location on the shoe requires the origin marking near it
Goods of Canada and Mexico take their origin for marking and Section 301/338 purposes from the 19 CFR part 102 tariff-shift rules
Leather Guides: footwear may not be called "leather" unless made of leather in the parts described; imitation, bonded, split or embossed leather must be disclosed

Footwear of exotic leather — python, alligator, crocodile, lizard, ostrich, stingray — is a wildlife product: it must enter at a designated port, be declared on Form 3-177 and cleared by FWS before CBP releases it; CITES species need CITES documents. Cattle, goat, sheep and pig leather are exempt

Shoes designed or intended primarily for children 12 or younger are children's products: lead limits for the materials and coatings, third-party testing unless CPSC has determined a material lead-free, and a Children's Product Certificate
Report the Chapter 99 headings with the line: the 2026 Section 301 heading for the country, China List 4A (9903.88.15), Japan 1986 (9903.41.10), Brazil (9903.05.01), Canada Section 338 (9903.03.14)

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. notes 3, 20, 30, 50–52

groups.label: Waterproof rubber & plastic footwear (rain boots, galoshes, molded boots)
groups.note: Waterproof means the upper is neither stitched nor riveted to the sole. Boots almost entirely of PVC pay 4.6%; most others 37.5%.

groups.label: Other rubber & plastic footwear (sneakers, sandals, flip-flops, clogs, slides)
groups.note: Value per pair and construction decide the rate: zoris Free, molded sandals 3%, over-90%-rubber uppers without foxing 6%, others up to 48%.

groups.label: Leather-upper footwear (dress shoes, boots, leather sneakers, sandals)
groups.note: Exotic-leather boots and shoes need FWS clearance. From Japan, these lines also pay the 1986 40% duty unless the shoe is an excepted slip-on or sports shoe; from Canada, 6403.91.90 pays the 50% Section 338 duty even under USMCA.

groups.label: Textile-upper footwear (athletic and canvas sneakers, slippers, espadrilles)
groups.note: The 141.89 invoice data decides between the athletic (6404.11), textile-sole and "other" lines. 6404.20 shoes with leather soles and partly-leather uppers pay the 1986 duty from Japan.

groups.label: Other footwear (wood, felt, cork, disposable, other uppers)
groups.note: Leather-upper footwear on soles of wood or other materials (6405.10) is covered by the FTC Leather Guides.

groups.label: Footwear parts (uppers, outer soles, insoles) and gaiters, leg-warmers
groups.note: Parts are not "footwear", so the 141.89 footwear invoice questions and the Japan footwear duty do not apply; formed textile uppers carry compound rates like finished shoes.

faqs.question: Are shoes tariffed, and what are the U.S. shoe tariffs in 2026?
faqs.answer: Yes. Almost every pair pays a base rate that depends on the materials and the price: men's leather shoes 8.5%, women's 10%, textile or rubber sneakers over $12 a pair 20%, cheaper ones compound rates such as 90¢ a pair + 20%, and shoes under $3 up to 48%. Flip-flops (zoris) and leather strap sandals are Free. Since July 24, 2026 a Section 301 duty is added by country: Vietnam and Thailand +12.5%, Indonesia, Cambodia and India +10%, the EU 10% in total, China 12.5% or 20%, Brazil 37.5%. USMCA-qualifying shoes from Mexico or Canada pay nothing extra.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on shoes from China?
searchedAs: tariff on shoes from china to usa
faqs.answer: The base rate plus 12.5% (2026 Section 301), plus 7.5% more on the 242 lines on List 4A. A textile running shoe over $12 a pair pays 40%, a women's leather shoe 30%, a men's 28.5%, rubber rain boots 57.5%. Flip-flops, shoes with uppers over 90% rubber or plastic, adhesive-soled textile sneakers and many slippers were on List 4B, which was suspended, so they pay only 12.5% on top of the base rate. The IEEPA duties that pushed Chinese sneakers to 172.5% in April–May 2025 ended February 24, 2026.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on shoes from Vietnam, Indonesia and Cambodia?
faqs.answer: Vietnamese footwear pays the base rate plus 12.5% (9903.05.84) since July 24, 2026: 32.5% on textile sneakers over $12 a pair, 22.5% on women's leather shoes. Indonesia and Cambodia pay +10% (30% and 20% for the same shoes). From August 7, 2025 to February 23, 2026 they paid IEEPA duties of 20% (Vietnam) and 19% (Indonesia, Cambodia) instead; the 46%–49% rates announced in April 2025 never took effect.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on shoes from Italy, Spain, France or Germany?
faqs.answer: EU footwear pays 10% in total when its base rate is under 10%, and only its base rate when that is 10% or more (9903.05.38–.39). So Italian or Spanish leather shoes, boots and sandals pay 10% — $100 on a $1,000 pair — and EU textile or rubber sneakers over $12 pay their 20% base rate. In late 2025 the IEEPA rate was 15% in total; it ended February 24, 2026.

faqs.question: Are there tariffs on shoes from Canada?
searchedAs: tariffs on shoes from canada to us
is there a tariff on shoes from canada
faqs.answer: Shoes that qualify under USMCA pay nothing — with one exception: women's and other non-men's leather ankle boots with rubber or plastic soles (6403.91.90) pay a 50% Section 338 duty since August 22, 2026, even under USMCA. Non-qualifying Canadian footwear pays the base rate plus 10% (and 70% in total for 6403.91.90).

faqs.question: Why do leather shoes from Japan pay 52.5%?
faqs.answer: Two duties stack. Japanese goods pay 12.5% in total where the base rate is lower (2026 Section 301), and leather footwear from Japan also pays 40% under 9903.41.10, a Section 301 duty imposed in 1986 over Japan's quotas on U.S. leather and footwear that has never been ended. Indoor slip-ons with thin soles and sports footwear such as cleated, ski, skating, wrestling, boxing and cycling shoes are excepted and pay 12.5%; Japanese rubber, plastic and textile shoes pay 12.5% or their base rate if higher.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on shoes from the UK?
faqs.answer: The base rate plus 10% (9903.05.81): a Goodyear-welted leather shoe (5%) pays 15%, other men's leather shoes 18.5%, women's 20%. No Chapter 64 line is on the UK exception list.

faqs.question: What is the HTS code for shoes?
faqs.answer: Shoes are in HTS Chapter 64, by material: 6401 waterproof rubber or plastic boots, 6402 other rubber or plastic footwear, 6403 leather uppers, 6404 textile uppers, 6405 other footwear, 6406 parts. The upper is the material with the greatest external surface area, the sole the material touching the ground most; then gender, construction (welt, foxing), use (athletic, work, slippers) and value per pair pick the 10-digit line.

faqs.question: What is the HTS code for sneakers and running shoes?
faqs.answer: Textile-upper sneakers with rubber or plastic soles are 6404.11: 20% over $12 a pair (6404.11.90), 90¢/pr. + 20% for $6.50–$12, 90¢/pr. + 37.5% for $3–$6.50, 48% under $3, or 10.5% if leather overlays cover over half the upper. Leather sneakers are 6403.99.60 (men, 8.5%) or 6403.99.90 (women and others, 10%). Rubber or plastic sneakers over $12 are 6402.99.90 (20%), and waterproof hiking or trail running shoes over $24 6402.91.42 or 6402.99.32 (20%).

faqs.question: What is the HS code for boots?
faqs.answer: Leather boots covering the ankle are 6403.91 (rubber or plastic soles: 5% welt, 8.5% men, 10% women and others) or 6403.51 (leather soles). Rubber rain boots molded without stitching are 6401.92.90 (37.5%), knee-high 6401.99.10 (37.5%), PVC boots 6401.92.60 (4.6%). Boots with a protective metal toe-cap are 6401.10 (waterproof, 37.5%), 6402.91.05–.30 (rubber or plastic) or 6403.40 (leather, 5%–8.5%).

faqs.question: What is the HS code for flip-flops and sandals?
faqs.answer: Flip-flops whose straps are plugged into the sole (zoris) are 6402.20.00 — Free. One-piece molded plastic sandals are 6402.99.27 (3%); other rubber or plastic sandals 6402.99.31 (6%) if the upper is over 90% rubber or plastic, otherwise 6402.99.49 (37.5%). Leather-soled sandals with leather straps over the instep and around the big toe are 6403.20.00 (Free); other leather sandals follow 6403.59 or 6403.99.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for slippers?
faqs.answer: House slippers have their own statistical suffixes under the line for their materials: textile slippers 6404.19.37.15 (12.5%) or 6405.20.90.15 (12.5%), rubber or plastic 6402.99.31.10 (6%), leather 6403.99.60.15 (8.5%) or 6403.99.90.05 (10%). Disposable hotel slippers made for one use are 6405.90.20 (3.8%), felt slippers 6405.20.60 (2.5%). Japanese leather indoor slip-ons that meet the 1986 exception skip the 40% duty.

faqs.question: What do HS codes 6402, 6403 and 6404 cover?
faqs.answer: 6402: footwear with outer soles and uppers of rubber or plastics (Free to 48%). 6403: footwear with uppers of leather and soles of rubber, plastics, leather or composition leather (Free to 10%). 6404: footwear with uppers of textile materials (7.5% to 48% or compound rates). 6403.99 is the catch-all for leather-upper shoes not covering the ankle with rubber, plastic or composition-leather soles; 6404.11 is athletic textile footwear.

faqs.question: How much is the import duty on a pair of shoes?
searchedAs: how much is duty on shoes
how much is import duty on shoes
how much custom duty on shoes
faqs.answer: It depends on the line and the origin. A $40 pair of textile running shoes pays 20% ($8) plus the country's Section 301 duty — $5 more from Vietnam, $4 from Indonesia, $8 from China. A $10 pair pays 90¢ + 20% ($2.90), 29% of its value. A $100 pair of Italian leather shoes pays 10% ($10). Since the $800 de minimis exemption is suspended, a pair bought online and shipped from abroad pays the same duty.

faqs.question: Can importers get the 2025 shoe tariffs refunded?
faqs.answer: The IEEPA duties, yes. After the Supreme Court ruled on February 20, 2026 that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, CBP opened CAPE in ACE: the importer of record or its broker files a CAPE Declaration listing the entries, and CBP refunds the IEEPA duties with interest, generally within 60–90 days. Section 301, China List 4A, the 1986 Japan duty and Section 338 are not refunded. Refunds go to the importer, not to retail buyers.
